thread.title: BlackBerry (BB) 3rd Quarter Earnings: What To Expect

author: Richard Saintvilus
title: BlackBerry (BB) 3rd Quarter Earnings: What To Expect
text:
Shutterstock photo Investors this week are looking to find out whether BlackBerry ( BB ), which has carved a leading position for itself in the fast-growing Enterprise of Things market, is still worth the wait.
The company’s stock price has fallen to its lowest point in more than a year. And although the shares appear attractively priced, would-be investors struggle to reconcile several fundamentals obstacles. Namely, to what extent can the former smartphone maker grow revenue? While the company continues to transition into the realm of enterprise software security services, the makeover has also been slow and painful to the profitability. Can it reverse these trends?
Before the opening bell on Thursday, the Canadian company is poised to answer some of these questions as it is set to report third-quarter fiscal 2019 earnings results. But with the stock down roughly 33% so far in 2018, BlackBerry not only must deliver a top- and bottom-line beat, its full-year 2019 forecast must demonstrate enough confidence to get investors to believe in the name again.
For the quarter that ended November, analysts expect BlackBerry to breakeven at 0 cents per share on revenue of $214.45 million, compared to earnings of 3 cents per share on revenue of $235 million during the same period a year ago. For the full year, ending in February, earnings are projected to be 14 cents per share, while full-year revenue of $892.85 million would decline 7.5% year over year.
Having ceded the mobile hardware market to Apple ( AAPL ) and Samsung ( SSNLF ), BlackBerry is still bleeding off revenues from its legacy businesses such as hardware and service access fees. The future of the company, meanwhile, rests on its software/services businesses, which, accounts for 81% of its total revenue. Along with BlackBerry Technology Solutions (which houses QNX and Radar) and Licensing segments, these businesses are producing revenues in excess of $50 million. But investors are keen to learn if this trend can continue.
Elsewhere, Wall Street will focus on — what I believe is — the company’s biggest competitive advantage: Its security features. Businesses and consumers alike are adapting to the new reality that data can be trusted to be stored online. However, this also increases the likelihood that the data can be hacked, hijacked or stolen. Will the company’s Q3 results or any associated announcement reflect that a move in that direction?
To date, BlackBerry has not shown it can effectively monetize its best-in-class cryptography, which could one day emerge as its bread-and-butter revenue driver. Then there’s the Enterprise of Things ("EoT") initiative, which touts hyperconnected things in a highly secure environment, which enables digital transformation. The management has spoken about EoT for several years, yet it has shown no meaningful impact on revenues. Will this be the quarter EoT shows signs of life?
Just as important, analysts on Thursday will look for cues whether the company can grow its customer base while churning out recurring revenue streams in the next few years. All told, BlackBerry still has a long way to go to earn Wall Street’s trust. But given its massive opportunity to turn things around, the risk-versus-reward on the stock now looks much more favorable than at any point this year.
